Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I want to bring to your attention that during the consideration of this bill in committee and again here in the House, amendments have been dealt with as to whether or not they go beyond the Royal Recommendation or do not go beyond the Royal Recommendation. In committee some of the proposed amendments were ruled out of order because they went beyond the Royal Recommendation, and I note in the bill before us that some of the amendments have the Royal Recommendations attached.
My point of order is the following: According to clause 51 of this bill, the government terminates its financial contribution to the unemployment insurance fund. Clause 51 of the bill repeals Section 118 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Section 118 of the Unemployment Insurance Act obliges the government to contribute to the fund for certain kinds of benefits, regionally extended benefits, fishermen benefits, et cetera.
Government Orders
By repealing Section 118, the government has, in effect, privatized the unemployment insurance fund. As a result of this legislation, the fund will be entirely contributed to by a compulsory check-off on workers and employers. All the moneys in the fund will be contributed in an obligatory fashion by workers and by employers, and no moneys will go into the fund out of general revenue as a result of clause 51 of this bill.
If that is the case, I do not see how we can refer to the Royal Recommendation which is necessary when you are about to spend moneys raised from the taxpayers of Canada in a general way from the general revenue fund. That is not the case here. No moneys will go into the unemployment insurance fund out of the general revenue fund or out of general taxation. What we are dealing with here from now on, if this bill is passed in its present form, is a fund which will be entirely contributed to by workers and employers in a compulsory fashion by a national check-off. That national check-off program was permitted by a constitutional amendment in 1940, following a Privy Council judgment which said a previous Unemployment Insurance Act was unconstitutional.
I want to submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is out of order in many respects. The consideration of amendments both in the House and in committee are out of order because reference has been made to the Royal Recommendation argument. I must say that some of the witnesses who appeared before the committee even raised objections stating that the government should not even amend the unemployment insurance system from now on because it is really a system which belongs to the workers and to the employers of Canada. The argument was made by several serious witnesses before the committee that the government could only amend the legislation with the consent of those who controlled the fund.
Before we discuss the various amendments to the bill, I would like you to consider this point of order with respect to the bill and to the changed nature of the unemployment insurance fund as a result of clause 51 which, in effect, privatizes unemployment insurance in Canada and which, by the way, this party very vigorously opposes.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to finally speak on this bill. I want to thank the hon. members for the lesson that has taken place in the last 10 minutes on parliamentary procedure. I am sure it will serve me well in the future.
I would like to address myself to this convoluted collection of amendments and to try in some kind of rational way to address the many, many things I am not going to be able to address in 10 minutes but that we must address, Motions Nos. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8,10, 11,12, 13 and 14. This is a very serious piece of legislation that is going to affect Canadians from coast to coast, from the Arctic circle to the 49th parallel, and we are having it compressed into a debate on one motion.
First, I would like to talk about the establishment of a new benefits structure. It is an establishment that replaces the three phase system now in place. The new maximum duration of benefits will be based on the weeks of work and the regional unemployment rate determined in accordance with table 2, et cetera, that is attached to the bill.
The extent of the cuts do not look like much, and hon. members from the other side would have Canadians believe that the primary intent of these amendments is to have Canadians go through some form of behavior modification, to use a term used considerably during the hearings. Behaviour modification is a 1984 Orwellian attitude that has no place in the Canada of today.

To suggest that Canadian workers need to have their behaviour modified; that Canadian workers are not diligent; that Canadian workers are not interested in working, is the cruelest, most despicable kind of PR that this country can do on behalf of its workers. To suggest that Canadians in areas of this country that have unemployment rates of 20, 30 or 40 per cent in some industries, could have their behaviour modified by requiring that they work an extra week or two weeks or three weeks before they are eligible for unemployment insurance, is the most cynical, despicable kind of attitude that I think we can muster for Canadian workers.
I thought that this House was the place where we had the opportunity to make people aware of what the government's plans were for the people. Canadian workers must be made aware of the kind of changes that these amendments to Bill C-21 will make to their lives, not to a piece of legislation that is mouldering in some library somewhere, not just to the regulation books in an unemployment insurance office. These amendments throughout Bill C-21 are going to have a direct and dramatic impact on the lives of hundreds and thousands of Canadian workers.
To suggest that those workers are going to be served- and that is another term that was used a number of times by the hon. members from the other side of the House in committee-is also an insidious type of suggestion. To tell people that you are serving them while you are grabbing something from them suggests to me that maybe we should take into this House a dictionary every day when we come in here and we should be looking up the definition of "serve". We should be looking up the definition of "behaviour modification". We should be looking up the definition of "abusers", because this government would have Canadians believe that most people on UI abuse the system. Possibly if not this government, but certainly a number of the members who have travelled with us on the legislative committee continually inferred that we, Canadians workers, were abusing the system.
I think it might be something that the Speaker's office would consider, to have on the desk of each member a dictionary so that we can be very clear about what we are saying when we are talking to the people of Canada and for the people of Canada.
Government Orders
It is very, very important that we consider the dramatic impact of these amendments on men and women, in our communities and to the communities themselves. What happens when a worker finds himself or herself with unemployment insurance eligibility cut back? What happens to the community? That worker, no longer eligible for the insurance program that he or she has paid for possibly for years and years of will often find himself and his family on the welfare system. Depending on the province, that will have a direct impact on the municipality or on the province.
The fact is that it has an impact. That impact trickles down to the community in every way. It trickles down to the small business people. It trickles down to the expenses of the municipality. It impacts on the school system. It impacts on the voluntary and social services communities.
I suggest that those kind of impacts have not been explained to the Canadian people. Those impacts have not been explained to the municipalities in Canada. Those impacts have not been discussed appropriately with the provinces.
I would suggest that some of the very serious amendments that we have put forward about the ability to bond for adoptive parents, amendments that would put this legislation in keeping with provincial legislation that requires adoptive parents to spend a certain period of time upon adoption with the child before returning to work, amendments that are not being heard, are the kinds of amendments that we should have. If we must live with this cynical, mean-spirited, cruel legislation, at least we could be concerned about the children that this legislation affects in the adoptive process.
The suggestion that we have one standard in terms of the bonding period for natural parents and a different standard for adoptive parents is something that I find very difficult to understand. We introduced an amendment which was ruled out of order because it somehow escaped the parameters of the legislation. I know I cannot question the ruling of the Speaker on that but I would at some later time like to seek an explanation because I do not understand how that goes beyond the parameters of this existing legislation.
The suggestion has been made that this unemployment insurance program is good for Canada at a time when, as a result of the free trade agreement, Canadians in various industries and sectors of this country are finding themselves faced with announcements of layoffs. We see ourselves facing in the workplaces the

October 16, 1989
uncertainty and the anguish that workers are facing. The suggestion that this legislation is good for Canada, and the hon. member for Saskatoon-Dundum started on that line of thinking earlier today, also defies one's imagination.
If one were to take a look at the numbers of people who are facing unemployment, if one were to take a look at the impact of the free trade agreement, if one were to take a look and go to talk to the workers who are facing lay-off with VIA Rail, if one were to go to take a look at the workers who are facing lay-offs because of mergers in the airline industry, if one were to take a look and go to talk to the workers from General Motors who have received announcements of layoffs, if one were to go to speak to women in industries that are now moving to the south including high-tech industries, computer-related industries, it would be very, very difficult for anybody in this Chamber to agree after hearing those people that this legislation is good for Canada.
We heard over 200 presentations almost entirely opposing some part or all of this proposed legislation. Yet, at the end of the day, one hon. member from the other side of the House said that that was because our friends did not come before us. When we had business associations, when we had major corporations, when we had groups that represent employers across the country and sectors across the country appear before the committee to oppose the legislation, to suggest that the government's friends did not appear before it is quite silly.
I would like to say, in closing, that it is incumbent upon this House to do everything it can to ensure that every clause of this legislation is debated adequately.

Mr. Speaker, today is World Food Day, a day to remind us that all people everywhere have a basic right to sufficient food to sustain healthy, productive lives.
Each year our world loses 11 million hectares of forest and 25 billion tonnes of topsoil through wanton, destructive ecological practices. Each year vast tracts of the world's productive land become desert. In Canada every year we lose thousands of hectares of our scarce agricultural land through soil erosion, salination, and urbanization.
Current policies of the government discourage family farming, national agricultural self-sufficiency, and the production of food for Canadians.
World Food Day also reminds us of the thousands of hungry Canadians who are receiving totally inadequate support from this government. These Canadians, most of them children, are not lazy; they are hungry. Food banks are flourishing. All of this represents a totally unacceptable way to feed poor and hungry Canadians.
In Canada there are one million people living below the poverty line. They have inadequate food. There are daily too many Canadian farmers unable to continue farming because of this government's defective agricul-

tural policies. Before it is too late, may I remind this government of the woman who 200 years ago ignored her country's poor and declared: "Let them eat cake".

Mr. Speaker, today marks the ninth annual World Food Day. This year's theme is "Food and Our Environment". The threat to food security is an increasing problem. The need to inform Canadians about global issues is now greater than ever. It is reported that the world produces enough food to feed all the people on the planet. We in Canada contribute substantially to the world's pantry, yet we hear almost daily stories of starvation and malnutrition. The problems relate to environmental degradation and food distribution.
The World Commission on Environment and Development has warned that without strong actions to redress inequalities in the distribution of the world's resources and the persistent abuse of the environment our very existence is in peril.
What is needed is an attitudinal change of dramatic proportions. This government's response to that challenge has been to reduce the amount of aid we give to tackle these issues. The last budget cut multilateral food aid by $32 million and bilateral food aid by $24.4 million.
Rhetoric will not feed the hungry of the world. It is time this government recognizes that Canada has the responsibility to play a lead in addressing the problems of food and our environment.

Mr. Speaker, this week is Co-op Week in Canada. I am pleased to rise and pay tribute to the co-operative movement.
"Together we make the difference" is the co-op theme. It reminds us that this country was built, not by dog-eat-dog competition but by working together. The pioneers of the co-op movement are grassroots men and women with the vision to realize that ordinary people can accomplish great things by pooling their resources and putting democracy into action.
Today 12 million Canadians are members of co-ops. We have the legacy of the Antigonish Movement, the Desjardins Movement, the Prairie Pools, Federated Co-ops and local initiatives from coast to coast in such areas as housing, health, financial, fishing, and worker co-ops. In this era when individuals and communities are increasingly losing the ability to control their own destinies through corporate globalization, free trade, and volatile money markets, co-ops make more sense than ever.
Therefore I call on this government to show some faith in grassroots Canada and to give the co-op movement at least as much support and encouragement as it gives its corporate buddies.

Recently in Sherwood Park Alberta the Eric W. Cor-mack Branch No. 277 of the Royal Canadian Legion dedicated a specially designed wall to the United Nations peacekeepers. The ceremony included dignitaries and a great many military service personnel and was a tribute
October 16, 1989

to the valuable contributions of Canadian soldiers, sailors and air crew in maintaining world peace.
On behalf of all of the people of Elk Island, I salute comrade President Don Crockett and all the members of his branch for their continuing commitment, hard work and dedication to the worthy cause of the Royal Canadian Legion, and I thank them for reminding us of our responsibility as Canadians in working for world peace.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of Parliament I deem it a privilege to present Fire Services Exemplary Service Medals on behalf of Her Excellency the Governor General.
The award is an extremely important form of recognition for Canadians who have made lengthy, essential and at times life threatening contributions to our communities.
Since the establishment of the award in 1985 the contribution of thousands of individual firefighters has been appropriately recognized. However, the current rules by which the award is made overlook a very important group of otherwise worthy and meritorious potential recipients; namely, those who would have qualified but retired from the fire service before the 1985 establishment date.
This is an injustice that should be rectified immediately even if it means retroactive recognition of some 2,000 or more individuals. I believe the cost to the Canadian taxpayer would be minimal in comparison with the contribution made, particularly by volunteers, to this vital community service.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of concerned citizens in Rankin Inlet, Arviat, Baker Lake, and Whale Cove in the Northwest Territories. Some 531 people in Rankin Inlet, 293 in Baker Lake, 187 in Arviat, and 72 in Whale Cove have signed petitions opposing the development of a uranium mine near the settlement of Baker Lake.
The petitioners are concerned about the protection of Inuit land, protection of the Inuit lifestyle, protection of the wildlife and renewable resources, and protection of the well-being of the residents of the area.
I urge the Government of Canada to recognize and consider the views of these petitioners who have asked me to bring their concerns to the attention of the House of Commons and in particular the government.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today 158 member nations of the Food and Agriculture Organization join in an annual observance of World Food Day. It is an occasion to reflect on an unfinished task-the eradication of hunger and malnutrition and the attainment of genuine food security for all people. This year's theme is: "Food and the Environment".
In Canada, World Food Day activities are co-ordinated by a World Food Day Association, an umbrella organization which brings together 235 non-governmental organizations, producer associations, provincial and local governments and many others. The World Food Day Association has from its inception received funding and support from the Canadian International Development Agency and Agriculture Canada.
Agriculture Canada and CIDA also have a long tradition of providing assistance to those in greatest need in the form of food aid. Even in times of financial restraint, Canadians on a per capita basis continue to provide more food in the form of food aid than any other country.
Just last week, the Prime Minister announced a $42 million economic package for Poland and Hungary. That includes $12 million in much needed food aid for Poland.
Let me assure the House and all Canadians that our efforts to help eliminate hunger will continue. Our efforts to educate people about the problem will continue. Our commitment and support are firm.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members would rejoice with me in the

October 16, 1989
Oral Questions
freedom that has come to Walter Sisulu in South Africa and many other black prisoners in that country.
While we rejoice at their freedom we also wonder why, at this time when it is obvious that sanctions are having an effect on South Africa, the Canadian government and the Prime Minister in particular would be drawing back from their commitment to impose further sanctions if apartheid is not dismantled.
It is obvious that it is not the intention of the new government in South Africa to dismantle apartheid. It is obvious that it is time for the Prime Minister to live up to his commitment to do that and to impose comprehensive, mandatory economic sanctions on South Africa so that what little progress has been made can be increased.
This is not a time to back down from Margaret Thatcher at the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Kuala Lumpur. Mrs. Thatcher is increasingly becoming marginalized, is increasingly becoming a sort of an international joke who may have been powerful in the 1980s but will not be powerful in the 1990s. The Prime Minister should not become a joke himself by kowtowing to Mrs. Thatcher.
Let us have comprehensive sanctions now and let us bring the day of freedom for South Africa closer, faster.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to bring to the attention of the House that Freightliner, one of the United States major truck makers, will construct a $32 million plant in my riding. This plant will create 600 permanent jobs and is expected to have yearly sales of over $400 million.
Freightliner chose this location because the region's citizens are good workers. Mr. John Mosier, president of the Canadian company, stated that the decision of the parent company in Portland, Oregon to allow Canadian expansion "shows faith in the Canadian operation and how they do business".
The members opposite feared that the free trade agreement with the United States would result in Canadian companies pulling up roots and moving south. The decision by Freightliner demonstrates quite the opposite.

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Recently, the prestigious National Planning Association of the United States published a report which said that the implementation of the free trade treaty could mean "a certain loss of autonomy in two important economic areas: monetary policy and taxation" for Canada.
I therefore ask the Deputy Prime Minister why the government negotiated a free trade agreement which would have such harmful results for Canada's economic independence. Why?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I understand the question properly, the hon. member is claiming that the trade agreement has these fiscal and social effects.
What we have seen so far is the following. We have seen tremendous job creation since January 1, under the agreement. We have seen tremendous new capital investment intentions, the highest really in history since they have kept records. There has been a 27 per cent increased capital expenditure in the manufacturing sector in the last six months as a result in part of the trade agreement.
More important, because of this wealth, because of this energy, social programs will be able to be maintained and strengthened in the future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw the attention of the hon. minister to a recent report published by the prestigious National Planning Association of the United States. This report said that the free trade agreement will limit the autonomy of Canada in matters of fiscal and monetary policy. For example, it states:
October 16, 1989

Increased capital market integration, as provided for in the FTA
between the two countries, should increase the volume of such capital
flows and therefore make Canada's exchange rate and trade account
more vulnerable to shifts in U.S. monetary policy.
I ask the Minister: Will he not admit on behalf of his government that more and more, day after day, it is clear that the free trade agreement is and will be a disaster for Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a country's autonomy in terms of fiscal policy and monetary policy is a direct result of the wealth of the country and the productivity of its economy. Under this agreement we have seen enormous quantities of new investment to put in place new plant and equipment for building a stronger infrastructure in our economy in the future. That of course will lead to autonomy in terms of fiscal and monetary policy.
More important, this particular agreement, by locking in a mechanism whereby we can retaliate against American actions which are unfair in terms of trade in North America, gives us additional autonomy that we never had before.
Mr. Gray (Windsor West) Mr. Speaker, the Canadian public will be very surprised to hear the hon. minister's answer. They have been led to believe by the government that there would not be trade difficulties requiring retaliation if this deal went into effect.
I want to ask the minister, specifically when he referred to job creation figures, why he and the government will not provide figures showing specifically how many jobs are created by the trade deal and instead are hiding behind the general Statistics Canada figures which make no distinction between jobs created through the trade deal and jobs created generally.
Why will the minister not take the studies the government produced before the election, which gave specific numerical projections of jobs to be created sector by sector, update them and give us the facts? Why will the government not come clean with Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that an analysis of this subject takes a proper period to do. The Minister for International Trade made this clear to the standing committee last spring. That analysis should be done carefully.
Oral Questions
In the meantime one can look to the future. How does one look to the future? One looks to investment in capital, investment in plant and equipment. It is up 13.6 per cent for business investment, over-all intentions; plus intentions are up 27 per cent in the manufacturing sector.
I know of no better example of the confidence that the business community and indeed the people of North America have in this agreement for Canada's economy than those particular figures.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister. I have here a copy of a release put out by the Prime Minister's office which states: "The Prime Minister announces growing global trade development strategy".
I also have here another release put out just about a year ago amidst the election by the Minister for International Trade which states: "Minister announces world market trade development strategy".
I also have another announcement made a few years ago by the other minister of trade called the "new national trade strategy".
Canadians would be interested to know, with all these different announcements for global, world, national trade strategies, what is the difference. Where does the difference lie? The programs announced in each of these releases are exactly the same. If anything the amount of money being announced is less than it was years ago because the expenditures have been reduced.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister: Why does the government keep recycling old announcements, old press releases, and old programs rather than begin addressing seriously the question of how we regain the markets we have lost over the last four years?
Was the Prime Minister's announcement in Singapore just another example of a Singapore sling?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to tell the hon. member that we have some news for him together with a reiteration of what this government has been saying for the past six months.

October 16, 1989
Oral Questions
The important news is that under "Going Global" $65 million will be spent for trade promotion around the world, $15 million of it in the United States. The rest will be spent in the Pacific, Europe and other parts of the world. This is what globalization means. The government has made a commitment to it, and it was announced on Saturday by the Prime Minister.
Something else has been made clear, and I would add this is news for the hon. gentleman. The Pacific Asia Travel Association, the biggest association in the Pacific with 4,000 travel agents, will have its first meeting in the history of that organization in North America. Guess where they are having it, Mr. Speaker. They are having it in Canada in March.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make sure we have the statements by the minister correct. He said that they are announcing $65 million for new trade development promotion in the United States and Southeast Asia.
In 1985, under the national trade strategy the funding was $70 million. Now considering inflation that is about a 20 per cent reduction. In fact what the government is announcing is about a 20 or 30 per cent reduction in the amount of money going into trade promotion and development efforts in the burgeoning Asia markets.
Once again, I ask the government why is it cutting back, why is it reducing and slicing the ability of this country to trade abroad at a time when our export markets have fallen precipitously in the last eight months?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will have to confirm the hon. member's statistics. I think he is wrong. I think the important thing for him to understand is the quality of our programs.
If the hon. member takes a look at what this government is doing in terms of international trade, he will see that we have programs that never existed before that are going to help us to penetrate foreign markets. A prime example is the whole border states program. Another program is put in place to take exporters abroad to help them with the new harmonized tariff system.
A third program will allow buyers from abroad, the Pacific, Europe, and the United States, to come to
Canada and be matched up with our international trade centres. None of this existed before. These are qualitative improvements in our over-all trade strategy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
According to a study prepared by the State of Pennsylvania, and I quote:

"Canadian firms are finding it easier to locate in the United States where the consumer market is some 10 times larger than her own and export back to Canada".

Will the minister finally acknowledge today that the loss of 60,000 jobs as a result of plant closings and production restructuring was caused by the Free Trade agreement? And could he explain why the United States is able to use the FTA to attract Canadian companies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like the hon. member to realize that 30 per cent of automotive production in North America is done out of Canada. Our population warrants 10 per cent and we are producing three times that.
In addition there are announcements eveiy day in terms of this sector of new plants, equipment and expansions in Canada which are considerable.
As announced by the hon. member for Elgin, Freight-liner will create 500 new jobs. It is a truck manufacturing firm in southwestern Ontario. I have here a quotation which states: "Hughes Aircraft expands in Canada". They see 500 new jobs. I have a quotation here from Honda Canada's president.
What about GM?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us talk about recent announcements. Let us talk about General Motors.
On Friday 2,500 Canadians who worked for the Scarborough GM plant found out, like 60,000 other Canadians, that their employer thought it was time to close down or rationalize production in the U.S. There is no doubt, however, the auto and auto parts industry is one the state of Pennsylvania has decided to target in its rifle shot strategy to lure production out of Canada.
After giving in to the United States on Canadian content, conceding any right to extract guarantees from firms locating investments in Canada, and refusing to give Canadian firms any further assistance in export promotion, can the minister tell Canadians precisely what he is doing to ensure that firms like Hyundai, which Canada has paid to come here, will maintain production in this country rather than shift their plants and sourcing to U.S. producers?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I respond on the automotive dimension of this, the hon. member is from northern Ontario and I think he would be very interested to know that last week the government under the FEDNOR program announced the establishment of Mirolin Industries in North Bay, a bathroom fixtures manufacturing operation. There are 319 jobs going there because of the strength of northern Ontario and because of the trade agreement.
The hon. member also knows that with the restructuring of GM in North America two things are happening. First of all, they are taking a look at their Scarborough van plant to see if it could be put to an alternative use. They have not announced its closure. They are studying to what uses it could be put. Even more important, Mr. Speaker, important GM facilities which have been based at Van Nuys, California are moving to-guess where- Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
The west coast fishing industry lost an important round when a month ago the free trade panel ruled
Oral Questions
against us with respect to the landing requirements for west coast salmon and herring.
The government has had a month. The final report is going to be released tomorrow. In anticipation of a similar ruling, does the government have contingency plans to deal with preserving the fishing industry in British Columbia, the 8,000 jobs, the protection of the resource, and the production of the industry?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has rightly pointed out, the government will be releasing the free trade panel response to the GATT decision. I think it would be appropriate if we waited to see what it says.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on October 4, the Minister of Transport announced that this government will cut passenger rail service in this country by 51 per cent.
Shame.

Since then, this government has tried to justify this position. As we all know, it is unjustifiable. In fact, the Prime Minister said in this House that the government was not going to destroy VIA Rail. On the contrary, it was going to save it.
The Prime Minister told Singapore businessmen yesterday that Canada was trying to get rid of VIA Rail. When he realized what he had said, he immediately changed the subject.
Why does the Prime Minister say one thing in Canada and say something else in Singapore? Why doesn't he come clean with the Canadian people and tell the truth?
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure my friend won't have any objection to my quoting all what the Prime Minister said, not just the part which the member used.
The Prime Minister said, "We are not trying to get rid-" But he said, "We actually have a 13.5 per cent

October 16, 1989
Oral Questions
manufacturers' sales tax. We are the only industrialized country in the world that penalizes manufacturers, so we have to scrap the tax". He was not talking about VIA Rail, Mr. Speaker.
Oh, oh!

A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. I thought my question had to do with VIA Rail. I wasn't talking about the sales tax.
The Prime Minister told Singapore businessmen yesterday that he was trying to get rid of VIA Rail. We know that from the remarks that were made. Why does this government not have the honesty to say to the people of Canada what the Prime Minister said abroad yesterday?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister in the last two weeks has said many times in the House of Commons that he wanted to keep VIA Rail. Moreover, he said that we want to keep a national network. It is also what we announced. The Prime Minister was here all the time when answering questions about VIA Rail. At no time did he say that he wanted to get rid of VIA Rail. He said he wanted to keep VIA Rail, but a national, sustainable and an affordable network.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Industry, Science and Technology. It concerns the government's attempt to finally recognize for Canadians the importance of Canadian-made scientific research and development. On Friday he finally recognized that the proposed takeover of Connaught BioSciences by Institut Merieux of France would not be of net benefit to Canada.
Why did the minister still give the company another 30 days to try to improve its bid? Why is the minister the only one who cannot recognize the fact that under no circumstances would it be in Canada's interest to have this company taken over by a foreign company?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, as provided under the law, I issued a statement indicating the current bid by Institut Merieux for Connaught did not meet the test of being a net benefit to Canada. I followed the law. I will continue to follow the law in terms of what is required
for reviewing any takeover of any company of any sort and will ensure it is of net benefit to Canada before Investment Canada approves it.

Mr. Speaker, the government should know that if this takeover is approved, the Canadian people will know that both Investment Canada and the government's rhetoric are jokes.

The minister knows perfectly well that the French government would never allow a takeover of Institut Merieux by Connaught.
Why is the Canadian Government doing nothing to prevent a takeover of Connaught by Merieux?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member without knowing the details of Connaught's operations, without giving any consideration to the nature of the vaccine, biotechnology and biosciences business world-wide, without recognizing the mergers of pharmaceutical companies that are going on around the world, without giving recognition to the advice of consultants and so on has said that we should not look at any of the evidence, we should not look at any bid that we should close our minds and make a decision before we review the facts. A closed mind decision may be appropriate for the hon. member. It is not for this government.

speakerposition: subtopic
N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. This morning's Toronto Star says as follows: "In an embarrassing slip of the tongue, Prime Minister Brian Mulroney told Singapore businessmen yesterday Canada was 'trying to get rid of VIA Rail'. Then Mulroney caught himself. Glancing at the travelling Canadian press corps he changed the subject.
The question I have for the Minister of Transport: Which is it, is the Prime Minister out to save VIA Rail or is he out to get rid of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said before. I said that the Prime Minister has been here for two weeks. All the time we were talking about VIA Rail. He answered many ques-
October 16, 1989

tions in terms of maintaining a national service across Canada.
Once again, I disagree with the interpretation given of what the Prime Minister was talking about. He was talking about sales tax which is not the same as VIA Rail cuts.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, throughout the whole debate on VIA Rail, we have been hearing one thing at one time and another thing at another time from this government.
Last night on The Nation's Business the Minister of Transport said that he had instructed management at VIA Rail to deal with laid off VIA employees generously. This weekend we learn that this government intends to weasel out of its contractual obligations of VIA employees. Is this the government's idea of generosity or will the minister stand in the House today and give a commitment, not only to this House and to the people of Canada but to VIA Rail employees who will be laid off, that this government will instruct VIA Rail to adhere to the contractual obligations in the collective agreement that deal with permanent lay-offs of these employees in a positive way? Will he do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if my friend remembers, because he was at my press conference, it is exactly what I said in my statement of October 4. I repeat. I said the government has asked VIA Rail to respect the collective agreement which has been signed with the unions. It will be done. I always said that from the first day that the collective agreement had been signed with VIA Rail that it would, of course, be respected.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment.
Some time ago, an assessment review panel was appointed to assess the environmental impact of the fixed link to P.E.I. Considering that many people in my area of Atlantic Canada are convinced that the fixed link to P. E. I. will have a dramatic positive impact on the economy of all Atlantic Canada, especially those areas of
Oral Questions
the Northumberland Strait, can the minister tell me whether the assessment review panel is in operation? If it is in operation, does it have any conclusions? If it has no conclusions, when can we expect some?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the assessment review panel has been set up since last April. In May we were provided with a bridge concept assessment by Public Works Canada. In June, the panel held public meetings. In August, the panel requested more information from Public Works. They will get this information and we expect a report from the panel to be filed before next April.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Immigration. A promising young reformist politician was murdered in the Philippines in 1986 four days after the presidential election. Rodolfo Pacificador is wanted for the murder. Yet this government has refused to deport him. Instead he has been released on bond. He has been given a working permit. Now he walks the streets of Toronto. He is a true fugitive from justice.
Meanwhile, the request of the Philippine government and the Philippine community in Canada to have him sent home to face trial has been unanswered. Why is this government, which deals quickly and harshly with penniless refugees, taking so long to decide whether a wealthy man is to be deported or not for murder? Is this not tantamount to a double standard? When can we expect a definitive answer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say that this is one of those cases that, because of the privacy provisions, I am unable to discuss in the chamber today.
I recognize the sensitivity of these issues for people with concerns around regimes that we as a government and as Canadians never supported. Let me say as well that we are not in any way harsh with refugees. Quite the reverse. Our humanitarian approach to refugees is still among the most welcoming in the world. I know there

October 16, 1989
Oral Questions
have been occasions when I have worked with the hon. member on some of these cases and I think he knows we do a good job.

My supplementary is for the same minister, Mr. Speaker.
When the new refugee system was put in place the minister promised that the government would have a faster track process to deal precisely with this sort of thing. But what is going on here? An accused murderer is walking the streets in Canada freely.
If the new system is so good, why does it take years to bring an accused murderer to justice?.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member would agree that one of the reasons that people like to come to this country is because we have a system where the law applies to everybody in the same way. If there is due process under way then that process must be allowed to continue.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister. As he will be aware, the Minister of Fisheries has refused again and again to say whether there will be a special assistance program for fishermen or plant workers whose lives have been devastated by the fish quota cuts in the Newfoundland inshore fisheiy alone. There will be 2,500 workers who will not qualify for UI this winter because of the drastic fishery.
Would the minister now admit that it is the government's shilly-shallying which is putting thousands of workers in Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada on the welfare roles? Is he willing to undertake to light a fire under the Minister of Fisheries to bring in a special assistance program without any further foot-dragging?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have been working with the Province of Newfoundland on the current situation in the fisheiy in Newfoundland. We have now received the advice of the provincial government, which has been working very closely with our officials. I expect that we would have an answer shortly on the situation with regard to the fishery. We are working as quickly as we can on this because we recognize its importance.

I thank the minister for her response, Mr. Speaker. I had intended to put a supplementary to her which I shall.
As she will know, like the cliche the proverbial round peg in the square hole or vice versa, whichever you like, the minister, I submit, with the new job creation regulations which are designed for Canadians in urban areas is forcing many thousands of fisheries workers who want to qualify for these programs on to welfare roles depriving them of a reasonable opportunity to get some income on standard make-work projects.
Would the minister indicate to the House that she recognizes that the job training requirements are not working in rural Canada, certainly not in rural Newfoundland, and would she undertake to bring in a program to cater to the particular needs of rural Newfoundlanders in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to admit any such thing because it is simply not true.
Where there is high unemployment, as the hon. member knows, there are no changes or very minimal changes in the unemployment insurance system. The whole role of economic development and training go together. If we are going to develop the economy on a small or large scale, then we need trained people. The two have to go together, and we are working very hard on that. It has had success in areas of Newfoundland just as in other parts of Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, three weeks ago the chair of the Finance Committee referred to seniors as being too old to need to spend money. Two weeks ago he said that Albertans were out to lunch on the issue of GST and suggested that they needed a grade five teacher to educate them.
This weekend our venerable "chair" remarked that business people who object to the proposed goods and services tax must be lacking in education and in competence. I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister whether these comments about a wide variety of groups and interests in Canada indicate that this government is

prepared only to insult those who oppose the GST rather than to listen to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make quite clear that the way the hon. member has expressed the question is not correct. The hon. member to whom he has just referred is not speaking on behalf of the government.
We have indicated on many occasions that we want to listen to as many views as possible on the goods and services tax. One of the ways that we will be listening to those views is through the auspices of the Finance Committee. Other ways we are listening is through our own members of Parliament as well as through opposition members of Parliament and directly through representations that are made to the government.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
The recent remarks about business people dismissed the valuable study and research that has been done by the small business community and organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and the Canadian Organization of Small Business. Can the finance minister assure this House that the concerns of the small business community in Canada will not be dismissed and that the government will accept the recommendation of the small business community and scrap this proposed tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the specific answer to that question is, no, that is not our intent. We have indicated that we listen to the small business community, its representatives and to all people who have a view that they want to express on the structure of this tax.
I think one thing that comes through very, very clearly and all the things that have been said about the goods and services tax is that we must make a move from the existing federal sales tax. The existing federal sales tax as was agreed, in two reports by the finance committee of the House of Commons, must go and the best option that we can look to is the goods and services tax.
We are now in the course of committee hearings and other forms of consultation to see whether there are ways of fine tuning this to make sure that we get the best sales tax system in the world today.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Small business in Elk Island and in other parts of Alberta is concerned about changing the federal sales tax. Small business people say the old way was simpler. Why should small business support the GST?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say to my hon. colleague how could the old way, the manufacturers' sales tax way possibly be simpler? We have 22,000 different tax treatments of 75,000 different manufacturers' goods. Twenty-two thousand different treatments.
Under the new tax, as the member knows, under the small traders' exemption, we will be exempting over half a million small businesses. Those that will be filing a remittance will be able to do so now-the vast majority of them-on one page rather than on dozens of pages under the manufacturers' sales tax.
Third, the cash flow is much better for small business under this than it is under the manufacturers' sales tax. You can get your credit back on your inputs before you sell your inventory-a tremendous improvement on the former tax-plus we have an administration rebate and we have a generous capital cost allowance for new equipment. Small business is better off under the GST than it ever was under the MST.

speakerposition: subtopic
Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister and it concerns the Gander air crash of December 12, 1985.
For four years, members of Parliament have been asking questions on this issue and for four years the government has been telling us that there is not a shred of evidence of any terrorist involvement or anything like that.
For four years the government has been telling us that there was nothing untoward and that it was invisible ice on the wings that caused the Gander air crash.
Why is it that we were not told until an hour ago that CSIS had conducted an investigation into the Gander aircrash years ago? Why were we not told this in the

October 16, 1989

House of Commons? What does the government have to hide on this issue?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said last Friday about Gander's crash that the government has done all that it needed to do about that crash. In fact, we did more. We asked a former member of the Supreme Court of Canada, Mr. Justice Estey, to conduct an investigation to see if we would have to have another inquiry on Gander. His decision has been very clear at that level.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It wasn't ice on the wings. You are right.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The member should look at the report by the judge another time. He did not understand it the first time, I believe. I think if you look at the report correctly, you will see what Judge Estey said. He said that it is likely that we will never know exactly what was the cause of the accident. But he said particularly that it is useless to have another inquiry. For that reason he recommended to me and the government to close the file, which is exactly what I did, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all, Judge Estey informed the Government that the crash was not caused by icing on the wings. That is my first point. Second, I want to ask the Minister of Transport or the Deputy Prime Minister why the House was not informed that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service had investigated this matter. Why were we never given that information? I would also like to know whether Judge Estey was aware of this investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, once again, all the facts, all documents and all the necessary information were submitted to a person who has a very high degree of credibility in this country. Perhaps the Hon. Member will agree that we can trust Judge Estey when he says in his recommendation to the Government that since there was no way to determine the exact cause of the accident, he did not see any need for a new inquiry that would reach the same conclusions. We therefore accepted the report, the case was closed, and we do not intend to reopen the Gander case, for very obvious reasons.

Mr. Speaker, it is to my great sorrow that I wish to inform the House of the marine tragedy that occurred yesterday in the waters of the Atlantic, a few kilometres north of St. John's, Newfoundland.
This tragedy took place during a search and rescue operation conducted by the Canadian Coast Guard ship, Sir Wilfrid Grenfell. This ship was called to Middle Cove on the report of the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary that three divers there were urgently in need of assistance.

Upon arriving on the scene, the Sir Wilfred Grenfell launched two fast rescue craft. By then, two of the divers had managed to make it to shore on their own. One of the craft had just recovered the third diver when it was hit by a large wave and capsized, losing all occupants. The second craft immediately attempted rescue, but no trace of the four men could be found.

I regret that thus, four men were lost at sea; the diver, Leonard Caul, and the Coast Guard crew; Gregory Peddle, Officer in Charge; First Seaman Raymond Wel-cher, and Engineer Pierre Gallien. Their deaths bring to four the number of Canadian Coast Guard members who have lost their lives at sea in service in 1989.
It was on January 20 that Tom Shelby, of the Coast Guard western region, lost his life while going to the assistance of a tugboat in distress near Port Hardy.
I am sure that all members of this House will wish to join me in extending our condolences to the families of the victims of these tragic accidents. We salute their bravery and dedication.
Their loss is tragic, Mr. Speaker. I believe all members would agree that they shall be remembered as heroes both personally and as representatives of the thousands of men and women across this country who place their lives in peril to save the lives of others. Their daily bravery is testimony to the finest and noblest aspects of the human character.
We are indebted to these men and their colleagues in the Coast Guard and indeed, we are indebted to all of their fellow Canadians who serve in the dangerous professions, for it is the selfless courage of these thousands that provides hope and security to us all.

I am sure that all members of this House will join me in extending our condolences to the families of these victims. We salute their bravery and dedication. Mr. Speaker, as you know the legislative committee of this House carried on public hearings on this bill for approximately four weeks in all provinces of this country and also carried on extensive hearings here in Ottawa. As a result of those hearings, 157 out of 202 groups appearing before the committee vigorously, strongly opposed this bill.
As a matter of fact, a great percentage of those 157 groups appearing asked that the bill be withdrawn and sent back to the drawing board to be redrafted. I mention that because a good number of the 50-odd amendments to Bill C-21 that were put before this House arose from the public hearings. These are not amendments that have been created in the minds of Liberals, these are amendments that were strongly urged to the committee by the witness groups that appeared.
Why did these witness groups opposed this bill in such large numbers? They did so because the minister, through the bill, intends to reduce unemployment insurance benefits by between $1.3 billion and $1.5 billion. She intends to take that amount of money away from unemployed workers; money they need to pay their rent, buy their groceries and pay for the necessities of life while they are unemployed.
Several impact studies that have been made on this bill, but the global impact study indicates that 155,000 Canadians would lose their benefits altogether as a result of this bill and that 775,000 would have their benefits reduced. If you have your unemployment insurance benefits cut out altogether or reduced and you are left without unemployment insurance, there are only two alternatives. You have to either go to the soup kitchen or to the provincial welfare system. That is not an option that we, as federal members of Parliament, should be imposing on unemployed Canadians.
In response to that, the minister and the government will say, yes, they are taking between $1.3 and $1.5 million out of the unemployment insurance fund, away from unemployed Canadians, but they are going to use it for training and development.
In many parts of this country unemployed workers are saying, "training for what?" They come from one-indus-tiy towns and there are no other jobs in those towns
except those that they were doing. They want to know if they will be trained so that they will have to go to Toronto or some other high growth area of this country?
That is a general introduction to this particular bill. This group of amendments which is before us, deals with special benefits, not regular benefits. These amendments deal with maternity benefits, adoption benefits, parental care benefits and sickness benefits. These are unemployment insurance benefits that go to individuals who qualify under those categories.
According to present law, maternity and day care benefits lumped together amount to 15 weeks. A pregnant woman could get 15 weeks of benefits either before or after the delivery of the child. The law also provides 15 weeks of benefits to parents who adopt a child. The present law provides 15 weeks of benefits to people who are sick and cannot work.
As you know, there were several court cases with respect to these provisions. The courts ruled in the Schwartz case and the McGuinness case, that we should divide maternity benefits from parental benefits because maternity benefits should apply only to the woman having the child, and should relate principally to her condition while she is pregnant.
They said child care benefits should be permitted to either the father or the mother, and consequently should be an additional type of benefit. As a result of the court decisions, I give credit to the government but it was obliged by the courts to bring the Unemployment Insurance Act up to date. It will now provide 15 weeks of benefits for maternity and 10 weeks of benefits for child care which can be taken by adopting parents or by the father or mother. It will still provide 15 weeks of benefits for sickness.
That is good as far as it goes, but I want to raise some serious objections to what the government is doing. To begin with, at the present time, adopting parents have 15 weeks of benefits. Under this bill their benefits will be reduced to 10 weeks. That is not acceptable.
I have moved in Motions Nos. 7 and 10 that these 10 weeks of day care benefits or parental benefits be extended to 15 weeks for all parents, natural parents and adopting parents, so that the child care benefits will be the same for all parents and will be the same as they are under the present legislation.

Under this legislation, as well, the government is saying there will be 15 weeks of benefits for maternity, 10 weeks of benefits for parental care and 15 weeks of benefits for sickness. However, under this legislation, if you have to combine them together, the government says the maximum can only be 30 weeks. There were many interventions before the committee pointing out how that provision is discriminatory to women. We are saying that because of their pregnancy they will not have full access to the 15 weeks of sickness benefits.
I refer to the very well prepared brief submitted to us by the National Association of Women and the Law. They say that while clause 9 would improve the act by increasing the amount of combined pregnancy, sickness or accident benefits to 30 weeks from 15 weeks, they state: "It is our belief that sickness or accident benefits should not reduce entitlement to maternity or adoption benefits, or vice versa". They then refer to Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states that there can be no discrimination on the basis of sex. They argue very strongly, and I am convinced by their argument, that this limitation of 30 weeks on sickness, maternity and parental care benefits is wrong. My amendment in Motion No. 13 would do away with that maximum.
My final remark is that the minister herself has introduced a amendment to her own bill in which she attempts to deal in a very selfish way with the brief put to us by adopting parents. The minister said she would be willing to extend the benefits for adopting parents from 10 to 15 weeks but, only if the child were six months old when it was delivered to the home and only if a medical practitioner or an agency that placed the child certified that the child had physical, psychological or emotional conditions that require an additional period of parental care. I think that is very niggardly. I cannot understand why the minister would not simply agree to increase the benefits from 10 to 15 weeks so that they would be the same as they were in the past.
I urge the House, government members and the minister to go the whole distance and permit 15 weeks instead of 10 weeks for adopting parents and for natural parents in taking care of their children. I would also urge the minister to remove this discriminatory clause against women which limits the total benefits to 30 weeks. It in fact discriminates against women because it says because

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words on the amendments to Bill C-21 before us, particularly those applying to adoptive parents.
One of the individuals involved in the court case referred to by the previous speaker is a constituent of mine. His difficulty was that because his wife was confined to hospital following the birth of their baby, he was denied any kind of benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act because he was looking after the children at home. The government was acting like a bunch of Liberals in trying to bring about that kind of justice to those individuals. It seems to me that if this government is serious about the kinds of things it says about the importance of the family unit, then the first thing this government should be doing is correcting those injustices that were in not only the previous legislation but in this amended legislation which has been before committee and is now before the House.
