I will give in point form some of the history which led us to the point we are at today. In 1976, for example, under a Liberal government, the maximum age for coverage was reduced from age 70 to age 65, cutting off a whole group of Canadians who had relied on that social safety net to provide them with an adequate social income after they left the workforce.
In 1976, also, the benefit rate for claimants with families was reduced from 75 per cent of insurable earnings to 66 and two-thirds per cent. The disqualification period for voluntary quits doubled from three to six weeks. In haste, one year later, in 1977, maximum weeks of benefits were reduced from 51 to 50 weeks. Eight weeks minimum attachment to the labour force for benefits was replaced by a variable requirement between 10 and 14 weeks.
In 1979 the benefit rate was reduced from 66-2/3 per cent to 60 per cent. People whose incomes were 1.5 times the maximum insurable earnings were now required to pay back 30 per cent of the benefits exceeding that threshold. You may be interested to know that that was the first case of income testing under that particular program.
At the same time, the government introduced a section that dealt with repeaters and new entrant provisions which established higher requirements for benefits to new entrants to the workforce, and for people who had claimed in the previous year. Then in 1980, the cost of operating the national employment service was shifted to employees and employers, and employers and employees became liable for all costs of initial and labour
force extended benefits. That is not too far off what this government is doing.
I remember when the then Minister of Employment and Immigration made a proposal in the House that took funds from the unemployment insurance program for retraining purposes. That is exactly what the government is doing. The government, however, says to people in Newfoundland, in Nova Scotia, in New Brunswick, and in areas of the country where there is already severe unemployment, that it is going to reduce unemployment insurance benefits to provide retraining funds. Retraining for what, Mr. Speaker?
In effect, what the government is proposing to do is have the highest trained group of unemployed people in the country, use, if it is justified in using unemployment insurance funds, for real job creation in those areas of the country where it is needed.
I had the opportunity to speak in the House on another matter a few days ago and I spoke about a recent visit I had made to Nova Scotia, to Cape Breton actually, a small community just outside of Sydney. In that community something like 60 per cent of the adult population is unemployed, and the average per family income in that community is about $24,000 a year. There is a large coal mine in that community that employs about 1,300 people, but it is threatened with closure. Here you have a community with very serious unemployment problems and this government is talking about reducing the amount of benefits these individuals will receive when they become unemployed, but the government is going to use the money to retrain them. For what? There are no jobs in these communities, and the jobs that do exist are rapidly disappearing.
I beg to ask the question again, and I wish I could hear some member of the government stand up and explain this to me and to people in those communities, what kind of jobs are these people going to be trained for? What kinds of programs is the government going to put in place to ensure that if people are government the benefit of the doubt, what kind of job creation programs are going to be implemented to provide those communities with meaningful jobs?
I have not heard any member of the government explain that to the House, even though there have been numerous questions in Question Period and there have been numerous questions raised before that committee that travelled around the country. Still we have not heard from the government. All we hear about is how the government is going to do the unemployed a favour
October 16, 1989

by initiating job retraining programs but without providing the jobs. Now, that does not make any sense to me, it does not make sense to people in these communities and it certainly does not make sense to the families of those people who are already unemployed and who have very little hope for the future.
I want to add whatever little weight I have and ask the members on the government side to open their ears and their minds and listen to those arguments, especially when we are dealing with this debate on a very serious matter for all Canadians. Even though many people may have jobs which may appear to be fairly secure just now, I would suggest that there are an increasing number of Canadians who do have jobs but who are becoming very concerned about their security in the future, not only for themselves but for their kids, their relatives, for the people who live next door, for the people who live across the street. They all know that in these times in Canada, particularly with the free trade agreement, there is a deep level of concern in the country about employment opportunities.
I see that you are giving me the high sign, Mr. Speaker. Of course, I always have great respect for the Speaker so I will wind down. Thank you very much for your usual kind attention. I would urge the government to get on with the business of the country and act in the best interests of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak to this package of amendments, but I should declare to the House that in a sense, I have a special interest in the proposals being debated, first, because the new legislation that deals with adoptive parents is something that I had changed when I was minister back in 1983 and had introduced the 15-week adoptive parent rule at the time because of a number of inequities. I should point out that at the time, it was supported by all parties in the House. I would recommend to members on the opposite side in particular the quite eloquent speech made by the now Minister of Justice, who, in supporting the legislation I introduced in 1983, spoke about the questions of equity and fairness, and the lack of discrimination that should be afforded
Government Orders
the parents of whatever child, whether natural or adoptive.
I also want to speak as a parent of an adopted child. One followed the other, and I did not in any way preview in 1983 that I would eventually become a parent of an adoptive child but I subsequently did. While I speak with a special interest, I also speak from experience, and I speak with a special knowledge, and, I would say, with a special concern about this subject.
I do not understand why the government is changing what was a good piece of legislation which provided the same treatment for parents dealing with new children coming into their households, whether by natural means or by adoptive means. It is as simple as that. There is no difference in the requirements. There is no difference whatsoever in the need to establish a bonding with the child, to deal with the very important period of establishment of affection and development of the child during that period of time. It does need a parent in the home for as long a period as one can be established.
It was a recognition, in particular, that the maternity benefits provisions and the parental benefits are not related to a medical reason per se, but are related to the question of the child itself and the relationship of the child developing in that family. The importance that we place in this country upon the development of the family has to be incorporated in legislation.
If the government says there is a difference in that family relationship, between an adopted child and a natural child, then so will the private sector say the same thing. A whole series of benefits will be thereby altered.
I also want to point out that it is very important in terms of the future of the child itself. Why would one want to say that there is different treatment being meted out to an adopted child versus a natural child? Saying that one parent is entitled to 25 weeks and the other to 10 weeks one is immediately saying that there is a difference in the process. There is not, Mr. Speaker, and I can say very clearly that when the child becomes part of that family, there is no difference.
I want, as well, to speak to the amendment that the minister brought in, which in a sense makes it almost worst. Now it is saying that an extra five weeks can be applied if there is a certificate by an agency or a doctor or some other official intervening. That is not the way to create a sense of fairness or equity. We are now introducing a new bureaucratic process into the exercise.

October 16, 1989
Government Orders
We are now creating a further impediment or barrier to that kind of economic and social well being. Why? What is the point of it? It gives more work to the agencies, to the medical practitioners. It creates more awkwardness, more cumbersomeness. It simply is bad law.
For a government that likes to pride itself on trying to keep things simple, trying to eliminate more bureaucracy, here is an amendment which, in fact, adds to it, makes it more cumbersome, more complex and, in fact, I think provides for an even further discrimination. It is saying that one only gets that extra leave if the child shows mental, emotional or physical problems. Who is the judge of that? Are we going to take a young child and say that that important period of having to be bonded with the parent is somehow based upon a problem and that it has to be certified? Is that the way we want the child to start life in the family, certified by a doctor or by a social worker that he or she is a problem child? Is that something we want on the record as a basis for trying to get leave? Any proper parents will not subject themselves to that kind of requirement. It only provides another major barrier, it is simply providing for an unequal and discriminatory set of questions that have no place in this legislation.
I suppose if we were talking about billions of dollars, one would say that maybe there is a reason for it. We are talking about maybe $1 million in extra costs at most, based upon the benefit period last year. Maybe it was $1.5 million, but the fact is that the amount of money that is involved is nothing, but in terms of speaking of the nature of a child's relationship with the family and the future, it says an awful lot. I say to you that this amendment only makes the matter worse, or at least it does in my view.
Let me bring up another point that was drawn to my attention recently in my constituency office while talking to parents. We all know that at some point soon, we will be seized in this House with the question of abortion and the question of offering a choice on children and what to do with them. Clearly, one of the options, an important option that has to be offered, is the question of adoption. When you are asking a young, unmarried woman or a single parent to face that question, one of the really
important problems that many face is whether to keep the child.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Single men.
And the men, that is true.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: I have a friend who is in that position.

In both cases, and I agree with the hon. member. The question is whether to keep the child or to put it up for adoption. I think one has to eliminate economic and social barriers to that option. If you are going to offer true choice, real choice, then take away the economic or social constraints on that choice, eliminate the kind of problems that a potential parent may see. I will have more to say about that during that debate but, surely, if you are putting a further barrier, a further handicap on the question of adoption, you are adding a further constraint on the choice as to whether adoption is one of the viable choices to be made.
It has repercussions way beyond just unemployment insurance. This particular motion speaks to an important part of family policy in this country. It speaks to how we look at children, how we look at the family and the relationship between them. I do not see the minister in the House, and I am not being critical, but I would hope those who speak to the minister would draw this to the government's attention and would say that it does not change the intent of the bill. This is not something that is going to do damage.
I do not agree with the intent of these amendments. God knows, when I was Minister of Employment, I fought for totally opposite kinds of views because I saw unemployment insurance as an expansive, inclusive kind of legislation and not one that tries to restrict or exclude, so it is a different philosophy.
The government may have that right, but on this measure alone, I think we are dealing with something that Conservative members previously fully adopted and supported in 1983. Why they would change their minds now, I have no idea. Why a worthy and distinguished member like the Minister of Justice would change his mind and vote for something like this, I have no idea, because he was very eloquent in supporting the 1983 amendments.
October 16, 1989

Furthermore, I would say to members generally, look at what this amendment does. Look at what they are talking about. We are simply saying that there is a discrimination. There is a distinction. There is a difference between the nature of a family relationship if the child is natural or adopted. I do not think anyone in this House or in this country wants to create that kind of discrimination. I would simply ask members opposite as I would ask members of the House generally to be very careful when they come to this series of amendments.
My colleague, the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, has brought in the proper amendment, to simply restore the status quo, to make it clear that all families and all children get treated the same. I would encourage members on both opposition and government sides to vote for that amendment. It makes sense from a family point of view. It makes sense in terms of the basic principles of equity and equality in this society.

Mr. Speaker, I wish I could say it is a pleasure to rise to speak on this bill today. It is not. I wish it were not here. I wish it would go away. I wish the government would go back to the unanimous recommendations that were reached by an all-party committee in the previous Parliament to truly reform the unemployment insurance bill. With the support of government members and opposition members from both parties, the government has chosen to go in a completely opposite direction, to take a punitive and blaming approach toward those who happen to be without a job through no fault of their own.
As we travelled across the country, we heard in city after city and town after town about how this bill will contribute to the growing disparity in our country between those who have and those who have not. It will make people who are the working poor even poorer and those regions which are poor even poorer.
This is exemplified by the fact that those with the lowest incomes lose the most in benefits. Perhaps I could just give a couple of examples. Those earning under $10,000 who are disqualified or limited in their benefits by this bill lose the greatest amount, on average, over $1,000, over 10 per cent of their income, when they cannot meet the new requirements of this bill. Eighty
Government Orders
per cent of those who lose under this bill earn under $25,000 a year. In many regions of this country, that is not even a poverty level income for a family.
The growing disparity is demonstrated by the fact that the highest loss per person who loses benefits or fails to qualify for benefits is in Newfoundland. If there are people who can argue that Newfoundland has the most thriving economy of the regions in this country, then I do not think they have their eyes on reality.
I wish to speak specifically to this group of amendments. The few saving features of the bill are not nearly enough to compensate for the tremendous damage it does to those who can least afford it. The few saving features of the bill are here, not from a desire on the part of the government to reform the unemployment insurance system, to make it better or fairer or to make it of more assistance to those who need income replacement when they do not have a job. They arise in fact from court decisions that left the government no option. One of those is the provision of parental benefits to natural parents as well to adoptive parents.
The courts have determined that in fact, it is contrary to the charter if natural parents do not enjoy the same parental and child care time as adoptive parents enjoy.
However, to introduce that equality, the government has chosen not to provide the same benefits to natural parents as to adoptive parents, but to reduce the benefit to adoptive parents. It has shown no interest in doing what is fair and just in providing to natural parents that which adoptive parents have enjoyed for a number of years and that which the courts ruled on.
Many amendments were introduced and many amendments are before the House to try to correct that basic problem. The only right and proper answer is for the government to take the 15 weeks that adoptive parents now enjoy and to ensure that the same benefit is enjoyed by natural parents.
Everything else the House sees before it, including the minister's amendment, are attempts to circumvent and not address the fundamental problem. The benefits should be the same for both and they should not be less than what the adoptive parents now enjoy. Any other amendment requiring certification, any other amendment proposing special adoptive leave are all efforts to

October 16, 1989
Government Orders
try to persuade the government, if it cannot go all the way, to at least go part way. It is not good enough.
In the bill, as amended by the minister's motion, adoptive parents are being robbed of what they now enjoy. Natural parents are not being provided that to which the courts have determined they are entitled.
The other inequity addressed by these amendments is the qualifying period for unemployment insurance. Can anybody give me a logical reason why a woman who becomes unemployed by virtue of a pregnancy and therefore unable to earn income should have a different qualifying period than any other worker in this society? Why should a woman in an area of high unemployment not be able to qualify, with the same number of weeks as any other worker who needs income replacement, when she has an interruption of earnings?
The waiting period is another problem that is addressed by these amendments. Again, the waiting period is a disincentive to use benefits to which the family is entitled. It is an economic hardship which makes it easier for middle or high income families to take advantage of these benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act than for low income families. Low income families simply cannot afford two weeks without income so that they can take advantage, for example, of parental leave benefits.
The argument has already been well made on the maximum period of benefits and I do not propose to make it again except to restate that improvements in benefits are not improvements unless you have every ability to take full advantage of, and to fully utilize those benefits for the purpose for which they are intended. An artificial cap of 30 weeks does not allow that to happen.
Finally I would like to say that the other equity provision that the bill addresses is to allow those over 65 to qualify for unemployment insurance. This again is a change imposed on the government by the courts that determined that discrimination on the basis of age is not allowed under the Charter and does occur under the existing act.
The government has failed to take advantage of this opportunity to correct a problem with legislation that was brought to our attention over and over again during
the hearings. That problem is the discriminatory way in which pension income is treated. Persons with pension income have that income treated as earned income for purposes of unemployment insurance. If they have a pension, they cannot qualify even though they are contributing, are available for employment and are intending to remain as contributors to the plan. That is not right. That is not just. In fact, we heard today in this House of a case of people being deprived of benefits that they were entitled to because they were misinformed on this provision of the act.
It is especially unjust when the same pension income is not treated as earned income for purposes of turning it into a pension plan or an RRSP.
I would like to conclude by simply saying that the government had and still has the opportunity with this bill to truly reform the unemployment insurance scheme, to go back to the all-party committee that reported to the House last year and to review again the changes that it proposed to the system, to come up with a scheme that is fair, equitable and recognizes the extent to which the government is responsible for unemployment in this country through various fiscal measures, and that it should continue to assume financial responsibility for unemployment in the regions of this country and for the poorest of the unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to this bill which unfortunately is before the House at this time. There are so many areas on which one could focus, but I propose to focus on this bill from a general point of view and in particular from the point of view of its effect on Saskatchewan.
This is a bill that hits the province of Saskatchewan and my particular community, the city of Moose Jaw and the area surrounding Moose Jaw in my riding, at a particularly bad time. Moose Jaw, like other communities in the province of Saskatchewan, is suffering through some bad times. Agriculture for the last few years has been very poor and agriculture has a very direct impact on the economy of the province of Saskatchewan. As well, we have a number of small businesses that are
October 16, 1989

closing, not only in Moose Jaw but throughout the province. We have workers who are being laid off.
This is a bill that the province does not need at this time. The policies of the provincial government, the policies of Premier Grant Devine, have added to the problems that exist in the province of Saskatchewan. I would remind you that it was Premier Devine back in 1982 who inherited a province from a New Democratic government, a province that was viable and vibrant and in the black, and indicated that you could completely mismanage the province of Saskatchewan and still break even. How wrong he was. Today, the province of Saskatchewan has the biggest deficit that the province has had in the history of its existence. Certainly the policies of this government have not helped the situation either.
High interest rates have had a disastrous effect on Saskatchewan. This government talks of the deficit and it knows full well that by lowering interest rates one percentage point it could save $1.5 billion a year. But in the province of Saskatchewan small businesses are suffering because of high interest rates and consumers are suffering because of high interest rates. Consumers are less willing to invest their money in consumer goods, especially consumer goods of any significant value, because of the high interest rates. Small business people suffer as well because they do not invest or are more hesitant to invest because of the high interest policy, and this is at a time when many businesses are struggling to simply survive.
The cuts in VIA Rail that are going to be taking effect in January of next year are going to affect the city of Moose Jaw to the tune of $1 million a year. One million dollars out of the economy of a city of some 36,000 people is a lot of money.
The government is further going to inflict harm on the economy of Saskatchewan and the economy of Moose Jaw by the goods and services tax which is going to further hit seniors, small business people, consumers, and workers in the riding and throughout this country. It is one more item that the people of my riding do not need.
The city of Regina recently conducted a study that indicated that fully one-third of people living in Regina are living below the poverty line. This is in a province that was a have province in 1982. It is now a have not province, and it is going down all the time.
Government Orders
This is a government that introduces changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, changes that are going to make unemployment insurance more difficult to receive and, when you do receive these benefits they are going to be at a reduced rate. In the last four years the province has lost 50,000 people; 50,000 people have left the province of Saskatchewan since 1985. As a net loss half those people, or proportionately the highest percentage of those people, has been between the ages of 18 and 24.
The future of our province is leaving. They are leaving because the employment situation is poor and they are waiting for governments, either federally or provincially, to put some investment into that province, to provide some opportunities for that province. Certainly this unemployment insurance bill weighs negatively upon that.
The unemployment bill further affects small businesses by forcing them to pay higher premiums, which is just one more item for many businesses that are struggling to survive. I remind this House that small business creates more jobs in this country than any other sector of our economy.
The city council of the city of Moose Jaw has been so concerned about this bill that it recently passed a motion which it has forwarded to the government. I think it is worth while reminding the House of that motion in which council voiced its opposition to the changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
It has specifically pointed out, first, that changes which reduce the eligibility requirements will restrict low income, seasonal workers from obtaining earlier benefits. Second, it is opposed to changes which increase premium costs for employees and employers.
The city council of the city of Moose Jaw does not pass such motions very lightly, but it represents the unified force that exists against this bill in the city of Moose Jaw and throughout the province of Saskatchewan.
In Moose Jaw housing starts have been drastically cut. Sales of houses are way down. Businesses are suffering and at the same time this government has indicated that the attitude toward regional program development has to be changed, that it has to be bottom line economics. This is a country that was built on regional development, that relies on regional development. Certainly the regions of this country deserve better. They deserve a

October 16, 1989
Government Orders
better attitude from this government than they are getting.
I find it somewhat ironic that my colleagues to the right themselves have been decrying this bill. There is not a single principle introduced in this Conservative legislation which was not pioneered under Liberal legislation.
The Liberals were the first people to take money out of benefits for training, and they even shifted the cost of the national employment service to premiums instead of government funding. The Liberals have been complaining about the way people are being treated with respect to voluntary quits, but it was the Liberals who first doubled the disqualification for those people back in 1976. As well, the Liberals complain about increased requirements to obtain benefits and about reduced weeks of coverage, but it was the Liberals who took both of these steps first in the 1970s. This government is simply completing the task which was commenced under the Liberal government.
We in this party are opposed to this bill. We are opposed to this bill because we like to see Canadians reach their full potential. We like Canadians to have the opportunity to reach their full potential. We like small business people to have the opportunity to invest and to prosper and grow. We also like people to have the opportunity to work in regions where they want to work and to be able to remain in places like Saskatchewan and Moose Jaw in particular, and not be forced to leave the province at the rate they have been leaving. It is an exodus from the province that is unprecedented, and it is going to have very disastrous effects on the future of our province.
We are opposed to this bill because it is not taking the direction in which our society should be heading. Instead of penalizing Canadians who through no fault of their own are unemployed, instead of forcing small business and employers and employees to pay more at a time when they are struggling to survive, we should be putting our effort into developing and maintaining viable regional development programs. Instead of its continuous attack on average Canadians this government should be allowing Canadians to reach their full potential.
We would urge that this bill be defeated.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal particularly with amendment No. 6 as listed in Votes and Proceedings, because several members have dealt with this matter of adoptive benefits. Indeed, we had several briefs that addressed this matter when the legislative committee was travelling, and the minister with this amendment is endeavouring to answer the requests of the various people who have appeared before the committee on it.
On behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration I am pleased to discuss this amendment to clause 9 of Bill C-21. It provides for an additional five weeks of parental benefits, fifteen weeks rather than ten, in cases where a child six months of age or older enters the home for the first time. To be eligible for this added benefit the claimant will have to submit a certificate from a medical practitioner or the agency which places the child with the parents. This certificate will confirm that the child suffers from a physical, psychological or emotional condition requiring an additional period of parental care.
This amendment addresses the special circumstances parents face when an infant has been institutionalized or otherwise prevented from going home for an extended period after birth. It will also be relevant in adoption cases where the children are six months of age or older. It is estimated that this covers approximately 90 per cent of the adoptions in Canada. When a child six months of age or older is entering a home for the first time, regardless of the reasons, it makes sense that a parent needs an extended period of time to welcome that child, establish daily routines, and develop a secure parent-child relationship.
This amendment is being introduced in response to representations that were made to the legislative committee during its study of the bill by those concerned about the interests of children and parents. Without this amendment adoptive parents would have seen a decrease in their benefits. At the time this seemed to be an unavoidable although not completely satisfactory approach to the government. What had been driving that provision was the need to treat natural and adoptive parents alike, in order to ensure conformity with the equality provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
October 16, 1989

The minister is very pleased that through the work of the members of the legislative committee on all sides and a number of groups which appeared before them this amendment is possible.
The government is committed to ensuring that the UI program is in sync with modem reality and recognizes the challenges parents face in combining family and work related responsibilities. This amendment, along with other provisions in Bill C-21 for maternity, parental and the combining of special benefits, will go a long way toward acknowledging current family and work situations.
I am particularly pleased to see this amendment go forward. I commend members of groups who appeared before us for the dedicated way in which they try to help children who have some disability. I was really impressed with the testimony they gave us and came to understand that it takes a little longer for a child who has a disability to become a part of a family of persons whom he or she may not have seen before.
I want to make a few other comments on the legislation, but before I doing so I would like to say that we heard more than 200 briefs, and many of them several times. I do not know how we are going to deal with this matter in the future. Perhaps the committee, in its wisdom, will decide that it is going to hear one national group give a brief. We had as many as 70 groups repeat almost verbatim the same brief over and over and over again.
Let the people speak.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: I do not know whether people consider that productive or not.
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: But, of course, when you are doing statistics it makes it appear to be very important.
Very embarrassing for you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: You will have your chance to speak whenever you want to get up on your feet.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we had many people appear before the committee. Many of their remarks will be featured in this debate by others. We had a witness in Toronto who spoke of the constitutionality of the bill and
Government Orders
gave us a long and very learned dissertation on how unemployment insurance became a federal responsibility through constitutional change.
By the same token, the person who made this presentation indicated that she thought perhaps this bill may not be constitutional. But when she was asked if she intended to pursue that point, whether she intended to mount a court challenge to the government on that, she said: "Well, I am not sure whether I want to proceed or not". Others who had her view brought to their attention were not that positive either.
The fact is the government has a legal opinion on the bill. It has been told by the Department of Justice that the bill is legal in all senses. What the whole matter seems to revolve around is what we mean by benefits.
Do we just mean dollars and cents by benefits, or do benefits mean training? Can they mean training? The major point of the opinion that the government received was that benefits can be more than money. They can in fact be training. If that training is going to enhance the ability of the individual to seek and secure employment in the future, then the UI funds may be used for training.
We have discussed the matter across the country with industry groups and small business groups. More than 50 per cent of small business groups say their greatest difficulty is in getting trained people to work in their businesses. We talked to people in industry who said that those who have high tech skills and saleable skills in the future will be the ones they will be employing.
Our attempt through this bill is to broaden the ability of our labour force to react to the demand that will be put on it by industry in the future to produce its products.
We have heard many comments made about mobility. It has been said that perhaps we should not be training these people to gain another skill because they may move away from the city in which they are presently living and seek employment in some other part of the country. For some reason everybody picks on Toronto. I do not know why that is, but I guess it is because unemployment is low in Toronto and what is loosely called the Golden Horseshoe.
The fact is that that is the history of Canada. People do not stay in one place for the rest of their lives. I was bom in Grimsby and remember moving to Kitchener, then to

October 16, 1989
Government Orders
Oshawa, then to Toronto, and then to Dundas because that is where the work was.
The Golden Horseshoe!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
The Golden Horseshoe; well you've got me there, guys.
If you look at the development of western Canada you will see that people came not from the west to the east but from the east to the west. Read our history. You will see that the success of the country has been in the mobility of people, people taking advantage of an opportunity that they see in another part of the country. That is what made this country what it is today, and that is what will drive it into the future.
I do not believe it should be a responsibility of the government to find an unemployed person in a village which is loosely referred to as a one industry village and keep that person in money until some other industry comes along and employs him or her. There has to be some initiative on the part of the individual to go out and seek employment. I cannot believe there is not a motivational change in an individual who let us say is married, has a job, has a car, has a house, has a mortgage, has some children, and becomes unemployed. Is he just going to sit back and say: "I can't do anything unless the government finds me a job. Woe is me. We will lose the car, we will lose the house, and I guess we will all have to go down to the soup kitchen the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace refers to".
I do not think that is the way it operates in this country. I think that retraining people and putting them into jobs that will be available or are available today-and we have lots of jobs available that cannot be filled-is the wave of the future, and that is the purpose of Bill C-21.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise in the House today to debate Bill C-21. As we have already heard there is great effort needed before the proposed legislation will be acceptable to all Canadians.
Before I get to specifics of the amendments proposed by my colleagues, allow me first to touch on unemployment insurance and welfare. These two safety net
programs are very closely linked. Unfortunately, in the attempts to reform unemployment insurance, the government will simply transfer part of the load on to an already overburdened welfare system. Let me explain.
The government's proposed changes make it more difficult for Canadian workers to collect unemployment insurance and shorten the benefit period they are entitled to. Obviously this will result in less people on unemployment insurance and more people on welfare.
For example, of the 83,000 people who are unemployed in Manitoba right now, 4,300 will have to go on welfare because they cannot qualify for benefits under the new eligibility rules. Another 24,000 will have their benefits reduced. In Toronto, as another example, metro taxpayers will have to pay an extra $2 million per year because the change will throw 4,500 people off benefits and on to the municipal welfare rolls.
In my own region of Ottawa-Carleton the regional government has predicted that it will be handling somewhere between 540 and 820 more general welfare assistance cases each month as a result of the proposed changes. At an estimated $550 per case, the increased cost to the region could be as high as $5.4 million per year.
Part of the proposed legislation will simply push many of the unemployed out of one safety net and into another. When we stop and think about the fact that in the Ottawa-Carleton region 67 per cent of all those on welfare are between the ages of 18 and 37, we can see that the second safety net is seriously flawed as well.
These Canadians need our help. It is my belief that something drastic must be done to get these people back to work. You cannot amend UI without improvement to the entire social welfare system.
Today I would like to concentrate on the proposed amendments to Bill C-21, in particular Motion Nos. 7 and 10. These motions have been put forward to correct a serious flaw in the government proposed legislation by re-establishing the 15-week benefit period for all those taking parental leave. This is a matter which is of great importance to many people in my constituency and throughout Canada.

Government Orders
If Bill C-21 is passed as it stands now, biological parents will be entitled to up to 25 weeks of combined maternity and parental benefits to provide care for their new child. Adoptive parents, on the other hand, will be limited to a maximum of 10 weeks to care for a new child. Adoptive parents will have lost five weeks from their previous fifteen weeks entitlement.
It is common knowledge that more and more biological parents are using their combined maternity and parental leave benefits very late in their pregnancy. The simple explanation for this is that they need and want to devote as much time as possible to caring for their baby after its birth. Yet, adoptive parents are not entitled to these maternity benefits and will, on top of that, be losing five weeks of parental leave. The loss of those five weeks is extremely important to any parent, biological or not. In my opinion and in the opinion of adoptive parents across our country this loss is unacceptable.
When we stop and think about it, Bill C-21 means that we will have very different maximum periods of benefits despite the fact that adoptive and biological working parents pay the same premiums for UI benefits. It is easy to argue that adoptive parents do not have the same pre-natal and post-natal needs of biological parents, but this is not to say that they do not have special and veiy real needs of their own.
In fact, the existing adoption leave benefit was put in place in 1983 to allow adoptive mothers to claim unemployment insurance benefits similar to natural birth mothers. The government of the day recognized that parental and maternity leave was not solely to allow the biological mother a chance to physically recover from pregnancy and birth; the legislation acknowledged the need for special worker benefits to care for a new child.
It is ironic that the member who is now the hon. Minister of Justice stated at that time, and I quote from Hansard of July 2, 1983:
Parents who adopt children face the same physical, mental, social and economic adjustments as natural parents. They often do not have advance notice of the date of adoption. I am pleased the government has brought in legislation to correct this discrimination.
Yet it is his government today which is putting forward legislation that will reintroduce the discrimination against adoptive parents.

Currently, adoptive parents are entitled to a maximum 15 weeks of benefits to take care of their child. Bill C-21 would limit this period to 10 weeks. The lost of these five additional weeks is a very serious matter for any parent, biological or otherwise. Mr. Speaker, this period should not be changed.
There are those who maintain that adoptive parents don't need maternity leave and benefits. That is not always the case. Everybody knows that more and more biological mothers combine their maternity and parental leave by going on maternity leave at a very late stage of their pregnancy. The reason is quite simple: They prefer to spend as much time as possible with their baby after its birth.
Adoptive parents have the same needs and requirements as biological parents. However, our present legislation prevents them from meeting those needs as natural parents do, because of the resulting loss of income. Ten weeks is not enough to establish a bond with a child that is practically a stranger. Experts in this area are well aware of the problems. Child placement services usually require one of the adoptive parents to stay home for at least six months after adoption. Why can't the government acknowledge this need as well?
Furthermore, the aura of uncertainty which surrounds most adoptions and the timing as well give prospective parents very little time to prepare for this event.
There is a tendency to believe that most adoptions involve newborn infants. That is certainly not always the case. Usually, adoptive parents do not know the age, sex, mental or physical abilities, genetic antecedents and sometimes even the race of the child that will be entrusted to them. Tremendous adjustments must therefore be made by adoptive parents who have to get to know their child after the adoption comes through. The uncertainty does not disappear once the child is placed in a home. Indeed, parents run the very real risk of losing their child if the natural mother changes her mind. In Quebec and Nova Scotia, for example, a natural mother has six months to reclaim her child. Of course, this possibility of losing custody of the child creates a great deal of tension for the adoptive parents. Biological

October 16, 1989
Business of the House
parents, however, do not have to worry about such an eventuality.
Given the short benefit period allowed adoptive parents under Bill C-21, we must conclude that the Government is totally unaware of the many needs of adoptive parents or, even worse, that it has simply chosen to ignore them.

With Bill C-21 the government also implies that the nurturing needs of an adopted child are not as great as those of a child living with its natural parent. In fact many adopted children require more time for bonding to be established. There are many reasons for this but I will discuss only a few. I can see your hand waving, Mr. Speaker, so I will move on.
Adoptive parents must be social workers, psychologists and parents all at the same time and at the very beginning of their relationship with their child.
If Bill C-21 passes into legislation unamended, the effect will be to discriminate between adopted and biological parents as well as between adopted children and biological children. Obviously this will have a major social and economic impact on adopted families and our communities. The legislation as it stands is regressive and discriminatory. I can only hope that the government will recognize this fact before it is too late and support the amendment as proposed in Motions Nos. 7 and 10.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and Motions Nos. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to rise in this House and speak on this motion. It is discouraging to be up here again fighting another rear-guard action as this government attempts to pick apart the safety net that Canadians have come to count on in this country.
Unemployment insurance was introduced in July of 1941. It was a direct result of decades of pressure from our political predecessors, the CCF, the farm labour parties, and so on through the 1920s and 1930s that saw the devastation which forced unemployment and cost individuals and communities. In the atmosphere of needing all the wartime production, all the labour force that the government could muster, unemployment insurance was brought in, in 1941, and has been an important part of our social safety net ever since.
There were two principles that guided the evolution of the unemployment insurance program through the years. First, unemployment insurance should alleviate individual hardship caused by unemployment. This was something that a person had by right of citizenship. Second, there was the principle that the effect of unemployment insurance and this particular aspect of our safety net should have equal impact across the country.
In other words, those regions of the country that were hardest hit by unemployment should be recognized in the way the act is administered so that those people would not suffer unduly because of the regions of the country that they lived in.
However what have we seen happen here? What have we seen the millionaire stock brokers from Toronto come in with now in terms of unemployment insurance? We
Government Orders
see a gradual shift to a charity model, back to the poor houses. We see food banks.
The hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam listed the number of people seeking help in food banks nowadays. We see people being forced off unemployment insurance through this measure on to welfare, which places a new and undue burden on municipalities and on the provinces. They also have a deficit problem. It does not help to reduce the federal deficit by increasing the provincial and municipal deficits and all the way down to increasing individual deficits, because individuals in this country are as deeply in debt as the government. Shifting it down to individuals, municipalities and provincial governments does not deal with the problem at all.
Another thing that this movement to change the unemployment insurance program is doing is forcing relocation of thousands and thousands of people. It is no accident that unemployment is high in the regions. It is not a fate of nature, the unseen hand, or anything else. It is the very real fiscal and economic policies that this government has brought in.
For example, policies like gutting regional development programs, especially for isolated communities, and making regional development accessible only to the big companies that already have access to all kinds of government programs. It is the result of an interest rate policy that funnels all the money from around the country into the big trading centres like Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver. It overheats those economies and then gets into a cyclical process whereby interest rates go even higher. Unemployment then rises in the regions of the country and the economic activity that could be expected there cannot happen because of interest rates.
Now we see a very miserly approach. We saw that when the member for Burlington was making his comments with regard to clause 6, the clause that deals with the relative benefits, paternal benefits between adoptive parents and biological parents.
First, it should be pointed out that this would not be here in the first place or that a government member would not be supporting it if it were not forced by the courts. Second, a approach like this that discriminates between different kinds of parents certainly cannot be said to be an equity provision.

October 16, 1989
Government Orders
When the member says that the provisions here actually cover 90 per cent of the adoptive parents, why then bring a miserly little motion that would discriminate against the other 10 per cent? That does not make any kind of sense at all, at least not unless you are looking at it from the perspective of millionaire's row.
I would like to deal specifically with Motions Nos. 4 and 5 because they deal most directly with the effects on regions such as the region I represent, Prince Albert- Churchill River, a northern constituency with high unemployment, scattered communities, and an underdeveloped economy.
The loss to this region can be figured in several different ways. The government came out with figures that said that the loss to the Prince Alberta-Yorkton UI region would be $4.4 million over the course of a year, each and every year. Global Economics said that the loss would be $11 million. When I checked into why this difference existed I found out that it was because government members were figuring behaviour modification into the equation. They were not taking into account the real numbers and how much people are actually going to lose; they were taking into account $6.6 million worth of behaviour modification in the region of the country I represent.
Whose behaviour is it going to be modifying? I did a little research on this. There are 600 claimants who fall under the clerical category, such as secretaries and office personnel. Those people often cannot move because they have family responsibilities and certainly cannot, as the member for Burlington suggested, move to Toronto, find a secretarial job and pay for the move with the earnings of a clerical job.
They are losing an average of $430 each. That is $258,000 worth of behaviour modification for secretaries and clerical personnel in northern Saskatchewan. Construction workers also have to modify their behaviour: 930 claimants, $613 or $560,000 worth of behaviour modification for construction workers in this constituency. This is totally unacceptable.
The chronic problem with the unemployment insurance program is determining the unemployment rates in regions such as the one I represent. For the La Ronge CEIC office the official unemployment rate is 13 per
cent. That is unbelievable. When you check into how these things are figured you can see why it happens because treaty Indians are not included in this. The surveys are done by telephone and only 20 or 30 per cent of the people have telephones and are inaccessible to any Statistics Canada surveyors. The actual unemployment rate in that area is in fact 25 per cent to 30 per cent, which would put them well over the cut-off line at 15 per cent. However, because of the way the figures are arrived at, that region will not be eligible for benefits that are its right.
Second, I hoped that when the whole Unemployment Insurance Act was being reviewed the whole problem of seasonal unemployment and the type of economy that exists in frontier areas of the country would be taken into account.
When I did research for this particular speech I found that although there are about 400 commercial fishermen in northern Saskatchewan, only 7 of them are registered with the CEIC although there is a commercial fishing benefit program. The reason is that these people not only fish but they do some line cutting. Their other big source of employment is firefighting. What has happened under that provision, as has been pointed out in the House, is that firefighters across the country are paid on a casual basis because it takes so long to get them on the government payroll, and it is easier to get the money by putting them on casual.
Consequently people are working many weeks through the summer. In many cases they work sufficient weeks to collect unemployment insurance, but because they are paid on a casual basis they are not eligible for unemployment insurance. Therefore there is a whole pattern of employment where people do some cutting line fishing, firefighting, and so on. Those people are working very hard.
There is an illusion that people who need unemployment insurance are lazy or not self-motivated. That is unfair. I invite members to go to that part of the country and see how hard people work and under what conditions they live. To penalize them and not deal with the problems in the UI system which affect them very directly makes a mockery of any kind of claim that the government might make in positively reforming the unemployment insurance system through this legislation.
October 16, 1989

The other argument that the government makes is that this new system is going to cost employers and employees. The government is withdrawing more and perhaps it will force some people to move. However, the government claims that the big benefit will be an increased amount of training, that there will be more money available for training as a result of this legislation.
Many Canadians appearing before the committee made the point that certainly training should be an investment that falls on the country as a whole and not an investment that falls on the backs of the unemployed. Even given that particular criticism there is no guarantee at all in this legislation, nor in any of the comments that I have heard made, that that training will accrue to the regions of the country where the biggest losses are being experienced.
There will be a real loss in our region of the country of $11 million. I know $11 million would buy a lot of training. I would be very surprised, in fact I will be watching very closely to see what portion of that $11 million gets back to that part of the country. The reason I am concerned is that I know that the government promised there would be the finest adjustment programs in the world when it came to free trade; people who lost their jobs would be looked after. The de Grandpre commission was supposed to recommend that all this would be done. It said existing programs should do it. Well, this is the existing program.
What is going to happen in a region like mine where there is a rapidly growing labour force of people who have never held a job and where there are unemployment rates of 50 per cent, 60 per cent or 70 per cent? I predict that the money for training is not going to go there.
The money for training is going to go again into the metropolitan areas where there are very visible job losses, for example to the GM plant in Scarborough, the Inglis plant in Toronto. Those are the types of priorities that the government is going to be setting for retraining because it is politically expedient to do so. That is where the national media is.
The Globe and Mail will report it and everybody will read here in Quorum that the government did wonderful
Government Orders
things in retraining, but no one puts in Quorum quotes from the La Ronge Northerner that says that there are thousands of young students coming out of the school system in northern Saskatchewan who need training and have never had an opportunity to participate.
I strongly support Motions Nos. 4 and 5 which would have the effect of equalizing the benefits that are available to people on the basis of the unemployment rates in their region and would not discriminate against people in our region of the country.
I also wish to strongly register that I am ashamed to be part of a House that would even consider taking such a gigantic step backward in Canadian social policies as this bill represents.

Mr. Speaker, after my hon. colleague has led us off on such a rhetorical note which makes sense nonetheless, it almost shakes the confidence of those who would want to see this House as a place where we would do things that are instrumental for the well-being of all Canadians and upon which well-being we construct a new future for all of Canada.
It is unfortunate that other members, some in my party, have had occasion to refer to some of the elements of these clauses that are absolutely contrary to that particular view. In clause 9, to which these several motions refer, the government is addressing itself to creating a fundamental attitudinal change among workers in the country.
For those of us who were not quite aware what the rest of the country does see in this particular clause, I would just like to briefly refer to a sentence from a September 11 article published in Vancouver. A member of the business community made a representation before the legislative committee studying Bill C-21.
I know my colleague opposite has an aversion to those who repeat positions given before a legislative committee, even though that repetition drives home points that are most valid. The repetition this time came from a member of the business community who said that Bill C-21 should have as its objective the creation of a mobile pool of jobless workers shifting across the country ready to plug into the needs of industry.

October 16, 1989
Government Orders
There are those of us who believe in an economic strategy, an industrial strategy for this country, one that takes a look at the resources and the needs of our nation and builds upon them for the benefit of all of its citizens, for the benefit of those people who would like to have work, and to create jobs on behalf of those who think that they can engage their energies and their vigour productively. Those of us who have been looking for that kind of initiative see instead Bill C-21 which does quite the opposite.
In fact because I would not dare to use statistics that the government so casually dismisses as being completely incorrect, erroneous, and unfounded, I will use government statistics in referring to the objectives of Bill C-21, especially in clause 9.
For example, this particular clause through its entrants requirements, restrictions of benefits, and lengthening of qualifying periods will have the net impact of causing 41 per cent of all claimants from Newfoundland to suffer reductions in benefits, 46 per cent of all claimants from P.E.I. to lose benefits, 40 per cent of all the claimants from the province of New Brunswick to lose benefits, and 49 per cent of all claimants from Manitoba will suffer a reduction in benefits.
I do not want to go on to the others because many of them fall into a much lower category, but it is important to keep those figures in mind when we address the objective of this government. If the objective is, as the hon. member opposite suggests, to put people back to work, the attitudinal change to which all other members have made reference suggests that the onus is going to be on the worker to locate the job. It will not be the result of any government program, any government strategy or great initiative, or any development of the market-place that generates jobs to which all workers will naturally gravitate. No. In fact I read those specific figures because they have a startling resemblance and relationship to other figures.
For example, using the labour market survey published recently and used as a reference by the government, it does appear that from the fourth quarter of 1988 to the end of the second quarter in 1989 that we are looking at a bill which says: "let's put people back to work by making them look for a job; make them accept the jobs that are
there". The natural question then is: Where are these jobs?
It appears that according to the labour market survey they certainly do not exist in Quebec because in those three quarters there was a net drop of 11,000 jobs. There was no growth in Prince Edward Island. There has been no growth in jobs in Prince Edward Island since the fourth quarter of 1987. There was no growth in jobs in New Brunswick. There was no growth in jobs in Manitoba. There was again a loss of 5,000 jobs in Saskatchewan.
My hon. colleague from Saskatchewan noted as well that there was a net emigration of 2,000 people per month. We are exporting the unemployment from regions less advantaged to other areas. This particular bill would suggest that the government is embarking on a grand strategy of job creation, a grand strategy of employment, a great plan to create a new wealth for all of Canada. It attacks those people in those regions where the results have been the contrary to expectations of employment growth.
That does not make sense. It cannot possibly excite the confidence of this House when we look at those government figures. They are not invented by others who would like to look at the gaping holes in this particular legislation. What comes through all those figures is an unfortunate description, and I use the adjective rather cautiously but I do it deliberately. There seems to be a petty viciousness. A less kind soul than myself might have looked at those provinces that I recited from these lists and said: "I think I see a political connection." None of those provinces returned a Conservative majority. There is nothing for the government to lose there politically. If the solutions are political to the problems of Canada, if the solutions are economic with political involvement then the government has nothing to worry about.
Those people have already told them what they think of the government's programs over the last four years. After five years of alleged unprecedented growth, I can stand here before this House and read those kinds of statistics. No, that sort of pettiness is unfortunately reflected in Clause 9 as well when we address what the government is doing in terms of looking for places where it can find funds to save and deposit to reduce its deficit. One of those has to do with people who perform not only a humane service but a social service, a national service.
October 16, 1989

They take upon themselves a personal responsibility, a great responsibility in my view, one that perhaps people like myself and many others throughout this country might not be able to meet were we put to the test. What they do is to take many young boys and girls, newborn, and provide them with a home. Because they do that, under this particular clause, we are penalizing them. We are penalizing those parents who take that step forward, those parents who want to adopt, who want to provide a home for children, all children, who they can call their own. They want to provide them with an environment where they can grow into mature adults, functional and productive citizens of this nation. We want to give them that opportunity so treat us like all parents.
An adoptive parent is a parent, period. It is unfortunate that before this House some of my colleagues have had to resort to giving a description of parenthood and to giving a description designed to encourage the government to recognize that parenthood is parenthood notwithstanding natural birth or adoptive situations and circumstances. That is a most unfortunate situation.
What we are doing with this particular clause is focusing on adoptive parents. We are going to reduce benefits. We are going to reduce the opportunities that they might normally enjoy under the former act. We are going to reduce their benefits in order to apply them to deficit reduction. It is an additional tax, an onus that we impose upon people for making the decision to do something that is socially worthwhile as well as personally satisfying.
We cannot through this Parliament, through this government, penalize those who have initiative that benefits all of society. Are we talking about a great amount? No, we are not. Several of the organizations and several individuals who appeared before us, and dozens of individuals who have written to me personally and to other members of my caucus have pointed out that we are talking essentially about a trite amount. When viewed in the global sum of $13 billion last year, rounded figures, for UI, we are talking about figures very, very close to $300,000 per annum for adoptive leave.
When we are talking about putting those kinds of parents through that kind of duress, we are talking about a particular principle. That principle says that the par-
Govemment Orders
ents shall not suffer but the children who are going to be children of adoptive families shall suffer. We have no right. We have an absolute responsibility to make sure that all Canadians are viewed similarly.
